Carbon fiber/epoxy composites are sensitive to lightning strikes due to low through-thickness electrical conductivity.
Four types of laminates were tested: unprotected, fully sprayed aluminum coated, locally sprayed aluminum coated, and aluminum coated on glass cloth pasted to fastener heads.
Impulse electrical current tests used 10/350 µs double exponential waveforms with peak currents of 31.3 kA, 88.4 kA, and 93.7 kA corresponding to lightning zones IIB, IA, and IB respectively.
The ablation temperature for carbon fiber/epoxy composite was set at 3316 °C, based on carbon fiber sublimation temperature.
Aluminum coating thicknesses of 0.1 mm and 0.2 mm were considered for protection.
Thermal radiation boundary conditions had an emission ratio of 0.9 and ambient temperature of 25 °C.
Element deletion in the finite element model simulates material removal when temperature exceeds ablation temperature.
The finite element model used ANSYS SOLID69 elements with coupled thermal/electrical properties.
Experimental and numerical results showed that aluminum coating significantly reduces lightning strike damage.
The electrical arc velocity during lightning strike is approximately 2 x 10^5 m/s.
Lightning strike can cause embrittlement, delamination, and failure in composite materials.
The impulse current generator can produce currents from 5 kA to 100 kA peak.
The aluminum coating can melt and vaporize under lightning strike, with explosive boiling occurring near 90% of aluminum's critical temperature.
The conductive electrical channel in the model was assumed to have a diameter of 10 mm at the lightning attachment point.
Glass cloth has very high electrical resistivity, allowing only minimal current conduction to fasteners.
The study used a 16-ply T700/3234 carbon fiber/epoxy laminate with ply thickness of 0.125 mm and total thickness of 2 mm.
Damage extent increases with increasing peak electrical current in the lightning impulse.
The numerical model incorporated temperature-dependent electrical and thermal properties of materials.
The lightning impulse current waveforms were based on SAE ARP5412 and ARP5414 standards.
The study combined experimental impulse current tests with advanced finite element simulations to assess lightning damage.
